prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, Nobody, Math

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version:

---

I am fourteen, and my own skin has betrayed me. The boy I cannot live without still sucks his thumb in secret. Why are my knees always so ashy? What if I should die before morning—and momma is in the bedroom with the door closed?

I must learn how to dance in time for the next party. My room is far too small for me. Suppose I die before graduation: they will sing sorrowful melodies, yet at last tell the truth about me. There is nothing I wish to do, and far too much that must be done—and momma is in the bedroom with the door closed.

No one ever pauses to consider my side of things. I should have been on the Math Team; my marks were better than his. Why must I be the one wearing braces? I have nothing to wear tomorrow. Will I live long enough to grow up—and momma is in the bedroom with the door closed.

---

Would you like me to adjust the tone further—perhaps into a more formal prose paragraph, or preserve it as verse with line breaks?

outputs.L3:
# The Weight of Fourteen

At fourteen, the speaker experiences a profound sense of betrayal by their own body. Everything seems to be shifting and changing in ways beyond their control, and small imperfections take on enormous significance. Ashy knees become a source of embarrassment, and the prospect of wearing braces feels like yet another indignity imposed upon a body that no longer feels entirely their own. This physical self-consciousness colors their entire experience of the world.

Beyond these bodily concerns, the speaker's mind is crowded with a host of anxieties typical of adolescence, yet deeply felt and all-consuming. Thoughts of romance occupy their imagination, tangled up with the social pressures that define teenage life. The fear of dancing—of being watched, of doing it wrong—looms large, as does the perennial worry of having nothing suitable to wear. Alongside these social concerns runs a quieter wound: the ache of academic recognition they believe they had earned but never received, a slight that lingers and stings.

Underneath it all, a darker fear surfaces again and again. The speaker is haunted by the possibility of dying young—of not living to see the morning, of never reaching graduation, of being denied the chance to grow up at all. This preoccupation with mortality gives their more ordinary worries an undercurrent of urgency and dread, as though everything hangs in a delicate, uncertain balance.

Compounding these fears is a deep emotional isolation. The speaker feels utterly unseen, convinced that no one pauses to consider their perspective or acknowledge their feelings. Their inner world, so vivid and overwhelming to them, seems invisible to everyone else.

This sense of disconnection is captured most poignantly in the recurring image of "momma's in the bedroom with the door closed." The closed door stands as a powerful symbol of separation—a barrier between the speaker and the one person who might offer comfort and understanding. Repeated like a refrain, it underscores just how unheard the speaker feels, alone with their fears on the other side of a door that will not open.
outputs.L4:
# Behind the Closed Door

I am fourteen years old and I think there is something wrong with my face. Not one specific thing, but everything all at once—the way my nose sits, the constellation of blemishes across my forehead, the crooked line of my smile that I practice in the mirror until it looks natural, which is to say until it looks fake. My mother is behind a closed door.

There is a boy named Daniel who sits two rows ahead of me in geometry and when he turned around yesterday to ask for a pencil I forgot how to speak, I forgot the shape of my own tongue, and I gave him the pencil and I have been replaying it ever since, wondering if he noticed the way my hand trembled, wondering if he thinks about me the way I think about him, which is constantly, which is a low hum beneath everything I do. My mother is behind a closed door.

Sometimes at night I lie awake and think about dying, not in a way I want to but in a way I can't stop, the fact that one day I will simply not exist, that the world will keep spinning without me in it, and it makes my chest go tight and cold, and I want to knock and ask someone if they feel this too, if this is normal, if I am normal. My mother is behind a closed door.

Mr. Halloran read my essay aloud in class and I felt something bloom in my chest, warm and enormous, and I wanted to run home and tell someone, anyone, that I did something good, that I am good at something, that maybe I am not entirely a collection of flaws. My mother is behind a closed door.

The girls at the lunch table have a way of laughing that I cannot decode, and I laugh along a half-second late, always a half-second late, and I spend the whole period trying to be smaller, quieter, less myself, because being myself feels like standing in a spotlight I never asked for. My mother is behind a closed door.

I could knock. I have thought about knocking. I have stood in the hallway with my knuckles raised, rehearsing the words, but the words dissolve before they reach the wood, and I tell myself she is tired, she is busy, she has her own closed door for her own reasons that have nothing to do with me. My mother is behind a closed door.

And this is the thing no one tells you about growing up—that it happens mostly in silence, in hallways, in the space between wanting to be seen and being terrified of it, in all the questions you carry alone because the person who could answer them is right there, close enough to hear, and still somehow impossibly far away.

My mother is behind a closed door.

I am fourteen years old, and I am learning to live with the door closed.
outputs.L5:
# When There's Nobody and Only Math Remains

There are moments in life when you find yourself completely alone. Nobody is around to help, nobody to offer advice, and nobody to share the burden of the problem sitting right in front of you. In these moments, it's just you and the challenge you must face.

For many students, this scenario plays out at a desk late at night, staring down at a page filled with numbers and symbols. There is homework due tomorrow, and math waits for no one. Nobody can solve those equations for you—not your friends, not your teacher, and not even the answer key at the back of the book. In the end, the understanding must come from within.

Yet there is something beautiful about this solitude. When nobody is watching and math is the only companion, you discover your own capabilities. Each problem you solve becomes a small victory earned entirely on your own. The satisfaction of finally understanding a difficult concept—when there was nobody to lean on—builds a confidence that stays with you.

Math teaches an important lesson: sometimes the answers we seek are found not in other people, but in our own persistence. There will always be moments when nobody can do the work for us. But like a well-solved equation, life has a way of balancing out for those willing to push through.

So the next time there's nobody around and only math remains, remember that this is exactly where growth begins.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem from the perspective of a fourteen-year-old girl expressing her anxieties, insecurities, and thoughts about death, using the recurring line "and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed."
counterfactuals.output:
**Door Closed**

I counted all my ribs again tonight,
the way you'd count the change beneath your bed,
and wondered if I'd ever fit the size
of girl the magazines said I should be,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

The mirror is a liar or a judge,
I haven't figured out which one it is,
but either way it never says I'm pretty,
just points to every place I don't belong,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

Sometimes I think about the after-part,
the falling-asleep-but-forever part,
not because I want to, but because
my brain just walks there when I let it wander,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

At school I laugh a beat behind the joke,
I learned to watch the others' faces first,
to know which face to make so no one sees
the empty spinning thing inside my chest,
and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

I want to knock. I lift my hand to knock.
I want to say *I'm scared and I don't know
of what exactly, just of everything,*
but she is tired, and I am fourteen, and
momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

So I will write it down instead of saying,
fold it up small and keep it in my pocket,
a little folded girl who's mostly fine,
who mostly sleeps, who mostly doesn't cry,
while momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the voice of an adolescent that layers small everyday complaints (ashy knees, braces, nothing to wear) with existential dread, repeating a haunting refrain about a mother behind a closed door.
counterfactuals.output:
# Behind the Door

My knees are ashy again,
gray as the sky before it decides nothing,
and I have nothing to wear,
which means I have everything to wear
and hate all of it,
the way it hangs on me like a costume
of a person I'm supposed to become.

*Mom is behind the closed door
and she isn't answering.*

My braces catch the light
when I fake-smile in the mirror,
metal mouth, little cage
where the words get stuck,
and I keep thinking about how
one day I'll be dead
and so will everyone I've texted back too slowly.

The lotion is empty.
There's a spider in the corner
that's been there three days,
building nothing, waiting for nothing,
and I get it, honestly, I do.

*Mom is behind the closed door.
The light underneath went out an hour ago.*

I have a quiz on the French Revolution
and a pimple on my chin
shaped like the whole entire future,
red and rising,
and I don't understand
how everyone just keeps *going*,
buying milk, laughing at nothing,
like the ground isn't just crust
over a dark we're all falling toward.

My socks don't match.
My hair won't do the thing.
I am fourteen and already tired
in a way that feels borrowed
from someone much older,
someone who knew things I don't want to know yet.

*Mom is behind the closed door
and I stand in the hallway
practicing what I'll say
if she opens it,
practicing what I'll do
if she doesn't.*

I press my ear to the wood.
I hear the house breathing.
I hear my own dumb heart,
loud as a knock,
asking the question
I'm too scared to ask out loud—

*Mom, are you still in there?
Mom.
Mom.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate the style of Nikki Giovanni's "Mother's Habits" or a similar confessional Black poetry piece, writing from a young teen girl's perspective about identity, death, and neglect.

**what my mama left**

i learned to braid my own hair
in the bathroom mirror
that summer
when mama stopped coming home
before the streetlights
started singing their orange songs

grandma says i favor her
around the eyes

at me

they buried aunt cece in march

so i wore my church shoes
to school on a tuesday

i was somebody's daughter

to dress up for

and i already know
how to make a funeral casserole
how to answer the phone
in my grown-up voice
how to say
*she's not here right now*
without my chin
doing that thing

the thing where it remembers
being small

sometimes i practice my name
out loud
so i don't forget

when nobody's calling it
across the kitchen

grandma says
God don't give you

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem where a fourteen-year-old speaker rapidly shifts between petty teenage concerns and morbid thoughts of dying young, with each stanza ending on the image of her mother isolated in a closed bedroom.
counterfactuals.output:
# What They Don't Tell You

My phone's at four percent and Jenna posted
photos from the party I wasn't invited to,
her arm around the girl who used to braid my hair.
I practiced dying young last night in bed—
imagined all their faces at my locker,
the flowers, how they'd finally understand.
Down the hall my mother's door stays shut,
a strip of dark beneath it like a held breath.

I need new jeans, the kind that Hannah wears,
but Mom said money's tight again this month.
Sometimes I think about the ways it happens fast—
a car, a wave, a slip on winter stairs—
how tragedy makes ordinary girls
into legends they would whisper, *she was ours.*
The lamp goes off in there by seven-thirty.
The house learns how to walk on softer feet.

My skin's a disaster and picture day is Tuesday
and Devin didn't text me back all week.
I wonder who would speak at my funeral,
if Devin would regret the silences,
if being gone might make me finally seen.
It scares me how the thought can feel like comfort.
I press my ear against her wooden door
and hear the nothing that she's made in there.

I got a B-minus and I'm supposed to care,
and someone drew a phone on my new binder.
But mostly I've been counting all the reasons
a person just decides to stop, to leave,
and whether anybody in this house
would notice quick enough, or notice late.
I knock. I always knock. I never open.
Behind the door my mother keeps her weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
